title: Massive Arms Exercises: Build Boulder Biceps
summary: NH demonstrates his three favourite biceps exercises: the close-grip preacher curl, a modified seated Arnold concentration curl, and the pinwheel curl. All three are done in a shortened, safe range of motion. He went from 11-inch to 18-inch arms in 10 natural years and says big arms are a matter of consistent, progressive curling.
claims: Big arms are achievable naturally; he went from about 11 inches at 18 to about 18 inches after 10 years of natural training
There is no way around it: to grow biceps you must curl
A close grip on the preacher curl biases the short head, which is underdeveloped in many lifters
On preacher curls curl the wrists inward rather than letting them extend, to recruit more of the forearm
Stop the preacher curl's eccentric when the upper arm and forearm reach parallel to the floor; going deeper just rounds the shoulders and is where biceps tear
Go all the way up until the forearm is vertical; keep hips on the seat
The preacher pad stabilises elbow and shoulder so you can go to failure safely and isolate the biceps
Finish a preacher set with a slow negative and an isometric hold at parallel until failure, then dump the bar rather than letting it overextend the arm
The long head grows from almost any curl and is rarely underdeveloped; the short head needs targeting
He avoids using tendon elasticity at full stretch on curls
Modified Arnold curl: seated upright, elbow braced on the leg, cupped or thumbless grip, range from shoulder to parallel only, ideally with a fat grip
Partial range is fine for biceps; do not obsess over full range of motion
He prefers pinwheel curls to hammer curls because hammer curls in front of the body over-recruit the front delt
For hammer-style curls grip the dumbbell at the plate end and tilt the wrist up to engage the forearm
The bottom portion of the pinwheel curl adds little; the stimulus is in the middle and top
Skipping the less useful range is better for recovery, injury risk and time
Train biceps intensely with as much volume as recoverable but spread across several sessions a week, rotating exercises
Small arms are mostly an adherence problem, not genetics; the biceps responds to progressive overload over years
exercises: wrists curled in; eccentric stops at parallel; up to vertical; finish with negative and isometric hold
